The rapid evolution of Artificial Intelligence (AI) has led to  a  paradigm  shift - moving  from  static  machine  learning models toward autonomous, goal-oriented systems capable of reasoning,  planning,  and  making  adaptive  decisions  [1]. Traditional  AI  approaches - including  rule-based  systems, conventional machine learning, and deep neural networks - have primarily focused on task-specific prediction and pattern recognition. More recently, Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated unprecedented capabilities in understanding, generating, and reasoning with natural language [2], [3]. However, despite these advancements, most existing AI systems remain fundamentally limited in terms of autonomy,  interactivity,  and  the  coordinated  execution  of complex  tasks [4]. These limitations have spurred the emergence of agentic AI systems, which move beyond passive inference  to  actively  interact  with  environments,  tools,  and other agents in order to achieve defined goals [5].

To  fully  comprehend  the emergence  of agentic AI systems,  it  is  essential  to  situate  them  within  the  broader technology  stack  that  enables  modern  artificial  intelligence [6].  Contemporary AI  ecosystems  are  not  isolated  software artifacts, but rather the outcome of tightly integrated layers of innovation  spanning  physical  infrastructure  to  high-level autonomous  applications.  These  layers  can  be  viewed  as  a five-tier structure comprising energy, semiconductors, infrastructure, foundational models, and applications - wherein each tier serves as a critical enabler for the subsequent tier. Figure 1 illustrates the progression of artificial intelligence  from  traditional  rule-based  systems  to  machine learning, deep learning and large language models (LLMs).

As agentic architectures increase in complexity and scale, the  need  for  standardized  communication  and  integration mechanisms becomes increasingly critical. Without common standards, developers must implement custom interfaces for every  tool,  data  source,  or  external  service,  resulting  in fragmented  ecosystems,  reduced  scalability,  and  significant engineering overhead. To address these challenges, emerging protocol-level  solutions  have  been  proposed  to  standardize how agents interact with external resources and other agents. Among these, MCP [7] provides a structured mechanism for accessing contextual information, tools, and data sources in a consistent and interoperable manner. Conversely, the A2A [8] communication protocol defines formal interaction frameworks that enable multiple agents to exchange information, coordinate tasks, negotiate decisions, and collaborate or compete  within  distributed environments. Together, these protocols represent the fundamental building blocks for scalable and interoperable agentic ecosystems.

As  the  complexity  of  agentic  AI  systems  increases,  a strong  need  has  emerged  for  standardized  mechanisms  that enable intelligent agents to interact effectively with external tools, data sources, and contextual memory. As AI applications  evolve  from  isolated  inference  models  into autonomous decision-making entities, structured communication  between  the  models  and  their  operational environments  becomes  a  critical  architectural  requirement. MCP  addresses  this  need  by  providing  a  unified  interface through which agents can access contextual information and external capabilities in a consistent, scalable, and interoperable manner [9]-[12]. Traditional integration approaches rely on ad-hoc implementations, wherein developers  manually  build  connectors  for  every  external service or dataset. While effective in small systems, maintaining such designs becomes challenging as complexity grows, leading to fragmented architectures, duplicated engineering effort, and limited scalability. MCP resolves these limitations  by  introducing  a  protocol  abstraction  layer  that decouples agent logic from resource integration. This separation  allows  systems  to  extend  functionality  without modifying core agent components, thereby enhancing modularity, maintainability, and long-term compatibility.

A2A communication frameworks represent a fundamental advancement in the evolution of intelligent systems, transforming them from isolated decision-makers into collaborative, distributed organizations capable of coordinated reasoning and task execution [13]-[16].
